meaning.evidence: Every beat survives: the weak back and the grindstone bet ("heave a grindstone up into a farm wagon if anyone wanted to bet him the cigars"), the shopping and Congress rant, the sunstroke, the "marble column with \"At Rest\" on it", the remarriage to Mr Gladden and the ironic misery. One added line, "Talk about never satisfied.", editorialises the ending and nudges the irony toward a judgement of the widow that the original leaves to the moral.

sense.evidence: Terms fit: "crook back", "tucker", "get the tea on" for getting dinner, "carked it", "send-off" for the funeral, "hard yakka", "nous" for gumption, "rapt" for general satisfaction. "punters" for people is a little loose (punters are gamblers or customers) but passable in a yarn.

authenticity.evidence: Reads like a real Australian telling it: "stuck with a great useless lump of a husband who wasn't worth a cracker", "every man and his dog was pretty rapt", "get a wriggle on". One stock bolt-on: "a fair dinkum good riddance of bad rubbish".

register.evidence: Level 4 weight throughout without tipping into caricature: "bludger", "dosh", "carked it", "down in the dumps". Vulgarity stays at dad level: "the lazy bugger".

tone.evidence: Keeps Ade's dry, deadpan satire: "So naturally she was down in the dumps, pinin' for the treasure she'd lost." The added "Talk about never satisfied." slightly spells out the joke rather than letting it land.

flow.evidence: Smooth, spoken rhythm: "Well, one day the husband copped sunstroke, too much of a bludger to shift into the shade, and the next day he carked it without breakin' a sweat." No pile-ups.

variety.evidence: Wide spread of terms with little repetition: "crook", "missus", "tucker", "wriggle on", "bludger", "carked it", "dosh", "punters", "hitched", "yakka", "nous", "rapt", "brand-spankin'-new".

essence.evidence: Unmistakably the fable: the lazy husband's jingoism ("the American people were better than every other nationality goin'"), the town's verdict, the ironic reversal and the moral "you keep on your own side of the fence" all intact.

problems.why: Added comment explains the irony and tilts it into a jab at the widow; the original lets the deadpan line and the moral do the work.

problems.quote: a fair dinkum good riddance of bad rubbish
problems.original: it was certainly a Good Riddance of Bad Rubbish
problems.why: "fair dinkum" as an intensifier here is a stock bolt-on; an Australian would say "a bloody good riddance" or just "good riddance".
"punters" means gamblers or customers; for townsfolk it strains a little.

A.summary: A natural, well-paced level-4 retelling that keeps every beat and the deadpan satire; only a small added tag and a stock "fair dinkum".

meaning.evidence: All points kept: "chuck a grindstone up into a farm wagon", the Congress rant, "copped sunstroke", "stuck it into a marble column with \"At Rest\" carved on it", Mr Gladden's store and runabout, "pining for the treasure she'd lost". The moral's "Woman" becomes "sheila", which keeps the sense.

sense.evidence: Most terms fit: "crook back", "tucker", "bone-idle", "carked it", "hard yakka", "nous". "every last zack" (sixpence) fits scraping money, if dated. "chuffed" for general satisfaction is right in sense though British.

authenticity.evidence: Mostly natural: "miserable as sin", "get a move on", "the lazy bugger". But "So everyone was pretty chuffed" is a British form an Australian would not reach for, and "If the sheila reckons he's all right" puts a dated, stagey term into the moral.

register.evidence: Level 4 weight with dad-level swearing: "what Congress was bloody thinkin'", "a bloody good riddance", "the lazy bugger". On brief.

tone.evidence: The deadpan irony lands cleanly: "So naturally she was miserable as sin, pining for the treasure she'd lost." No added commentary.

flow.evidence: Reads smoothly aloud: "Then one day the husband copped sunstroke, being too bone-idle to shift into the shade, and the next day he carked it without lifting a finger."

variety.evidence: Good spread: "crook", "missus", "tucker", "park himself", "bone-idle", "carked it", "zack", "hitched", "yakka", "nous", "sheila". "bloody" appears twice, not leaned on.

essence.evidence: The fable's shape and point intact, from "there was this bloke with a crook back" to "you stay on your own side of the fence".

problems.why: "chuffed" is British; an Australian would say "rapt" or "stoked".

problems.quote: If the sheila reckons he's all right
problems.original: If the Woman thinks he's All Right
problems.why: "sheila" is dated and reads as tourist colour in the moral, where plain "woman" or "missus" would sit better.

B.summary: A clean, faithful level-4 retelling with the satire intact; a British "chuffed" and a stagey "sheila" are the only blemishes.

meaning.evidence: Mostly the original text verbatim, so facts survive, but "say that he couldn't see what Parliament House wuz thinkin' of" swaps Congress for an Australian parliament while keeping "Uncle Sam" and "the American People", which muddles who he is ranting about.

sense.evidence: "Parliament House" takes the wrong referent for an American's complaint about Congress. Other swaps fit: "get tea", "dosh", "nous enough". "punters" for people strains.

authenticity.evidence: The few Aussie insertions sit awkwardly in the archaic capitalised prose: "it was defo a Good Riddance of Bad Rubbish" ("defo" is British slang), "He knocked together a brand-spankin'-new House", and the tic "Mind you" bolted on.

register.evidence: Far lighter than level 4: most sentences are left as written, e.g. "Nearly Everybody Sympathized with her, because she had to put up with such a big Hulk of a no-account Husband." and "Once in a Country Town there was a Man with a Weak Back."

tone.evidence: The satirical deadpan of the original survives because the original is mostly kept, though the broken "Mind you, Consequently, she was down in the dumps" blunts the final irony.

flow.evidence: Clunky joins from inserted openers: "Mind you, he was willing to divide the Labor, however;" and "Mind you, Consequently, she was down in the dumps".

variety.evidence: Leans on the same openers: "Mind you," twice, "Now," twice, "Well,"; few distinct terms.

essence.evidence: Recognisably the fable since it is largely the original, but the transplanted "Parliament House" and filler openers flatten it rather than retell it.

problems.quote: what Parliament House wuz thinkin' of
problems.why: Localises Congress while the rest stays American (Uncle Sam, Alaskan Boundary); wrong referent.

problems.quote: Mind you, Consequently, she was down in the dumps
problems.why: Opener bolted onto a connective; broken grammar that spoils the punchline.

C.summary: Largely the original with a few awkward swaps and filler openers; far too light for level 4 and clunky where it intervenes.
